title: Episode 145: James A. Garfield: The Canal Boy of Cuyahoga and the Dark Horse of 1880

James Abram Garfield was the last of the American presidents born in a log cabin—and arguably the most intellectually gifted man ever to occupy the executive mansion. Orphaned in infancy in the dense frontier forests of Ohio, he worked as a barefoot teenager driving canal mules along the Ohio and Erie Canal before falling overboard, surviving a miraculous brush with drowning, and dedicating his life to education. Garfield became a professor of classical Greek and Latin at age twenty-five, a Disciples of Christ preacher, an ambidextrous mathematician who discovered an original proof of the Pythagorean Theorem, and a heroic Union general at Middle Creek and Chickamauga. This is the extraordinary saga of his rise and the dramatic 36-ballot deadlock at the 1880 Republican National Convention where Garfield entered to nominate another man—and walked out as the nominee for President of the United States.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we begin our two-part journey into the life and tragic fate of James A. Garfield. He was a polymath of towering intellect: a frontier canal boy who mastered Greek and Latin, a devout preacher, a battlefield hero of the Civil War, and the ultimate dark horse candidate in American political history. Here is George with the full story of James A. Garfield's rise to greatness.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE WILDERNESS OF ORANGE TOWNSHIP
In November 1831, in a rough twenty-by-thirty-foot log cabin chinked with clay in Orange Township, Ohio, James Abram Garfield entered the world into grinding wilderness poverty. When James was just eighteen months old, a terrifying forest fire swept through the township. His father Abram, a rugged wrestler and farmer, fought the flames for twenty-four hours to save their tiny clearing, but collapsed from exhaustion and pneumonia, dying days later at age thirty-three. Left a widow with four small children and a heavily mortgaged farm, Eliza Ballou Garfield refused to give up her children to neighbors. She split cedar rails with her own hands, harvested corn in her bare feet, and raised James on a steady diet of Bible verses, Shakespeare, and ruthless self-reliance.

James grew into an enormous, awkward boy with a head of unruly sandy hair and broad, muscular shoulders. Taunted by schoolyard bullies for his fatherless poverty and patched homespun clothes, Garfield fought back with ferocity, earning a reputation as a boy who never started a brawl but never yielded an inch in one. Obsessed with nautical adventure novels about pirates and naval heroes, sixteen-year-old James left the farm in 1848, determined to go to sea. Walking to Cleveland, he was rejected by lake captains for his greenness, so he hired on as a driver boy on the Ohio and Erie Canal for twelve dollars a month, leading mules along the muddy towpath between Cleveland and Pittsburgh.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE MIRACLE ON THE TOWPATH AND THE SCHOLAR'S AWAKENING
Canal life was rough, drunken, and brutal. Over six weeks, Garfield fell into the murky, sewage-laden canal waters fourteen times. Then came the night that altered the trajectory of his life. Around midnight on a pitch-black stretch of the canal, Garfield was alone on the deck of the coal barge when a heavy rope snagged on a cleat. As he strained to free it, the rope snapped taut and catapulted him backward into the freezing, deep water. No one on board heard his splash; the heavy barge drifted steadily away into the darkness. Unable to swim well, Garfield flailed in the cold black water, sinking beneath the surface.

Desperately sweeping his hands through the water, his fingers caught a trailing coil of rope that had accidentally uncoiled from the deck. He hauled himself up hand-over-hand, coughing and shivering on the deck. Examining the rope in the lantern light, he noticed that it had wedged itself into a narrow crack between the deck planks by a single fray—holding fast under his weight. Had it slipped an inch, he would have drowned in the dark. Convinced that Providence had spared his life for some higher purpose, Garfield returned home to his mother, who had spent the night praying for him. Eliza gave him her life savings—seventeen dollars—and begged him to abandon the canals and go to school. Garfield enrolled at the Geauga Seminary in Chester, Ohio, working as a carpenter and janitor to pay his tuition, and fell madly in love with books.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE POLYMATH OF HIRAM COLLEGE
Garfield's intellectual appetite was insatiable. He possessed a photographic memory and an astonishing capacity for languages. At the Western Reserve Eclectic Institute (later Hiram College), he mastered classical Greek and Latin so thoroughly that by his second term, the school hired him as a tutor to teach students older than himself. He went on to Williams College in Massachusetts, where he blossomed under the mentorship of legendary college president Mark Hopkins. Garfield graduated with highest honors, and at age twenty-six, was chosen as the president of Hiram College.

Garfield was a true nineteenth-century polymath. He was ordained as a lay minister in the Disciples of Christ, delivering eloquent, passionate sermons across northeastern Ohio. He possessed an extraordinary ambidextrous party trick: he could write in Greek with his left hand while simultaneously writing in Latin with his right hand. He was an avid student of higher mathematics; later, while serving as a congressman, he developed an original, elegant trapezoidal proof of the Pythagorean Theorem that was published in the New England Journal of Education. Yet despite his scholarly brilliance, Garfield was warmly approachable, radiating an infectious boyish enthusiasm that endeared him to everyone he met. In 1858, he married Lucretia 'Crete' Rudolph, a brilliant, quiet fellow student whose intellectual companionship became the anchor of his life.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE PREACHER GOES TO WAR
When the Civil War erupted in 1861, Garfield was serving in the Ohio State Senate as a staunch, outspoken abolitionist. He believed slavery was a moral abomination that must be purged by blood and fire. Commissioned as colonel of the 42nd Ohio Volunteer Infantry, Garfield recruited his regiment heavily from his former students and teachers at Hiram College. Though he had never commanded a soldier in the field, Garfield devoured military treatises, memorizing infantry tactics overnight. Dispatched to the rugged, mountainous wilderness of eastern Kentucky in the winter of 1861, Garfield was given an impossible task: clear a superior Confederate force commanded by General Humphrey Marshall out of the Big Sandy River valley.

At the Battle of Middle Creek in January 1862, Garfield executed a brilliant tactical bluff. Facing twice his numbers entrenched on steep mountain ridges, Garfield sent small detachments charging up different ridges at staggered intervals, shouting orders to imaginary reinforcements. Convinced that massive Union armies were surrounding him, Marshall panicked, burned his supplies, and retreated into Virginia. For this stunning victory, Lincoln promoted Garfield to brigadier general at age thirty—the youngest general in the Union army. At the bloody Battle of Chickamauga in September 1863, when the Union right wing collapsed and General William Rosecrans fled the field, Garfield galloped through a storm of enemy fire across Horseshoe Ridge to carry crucial orders to General George H. Thomas, helping Thomas earn his immortal title as the 'Rock of Chickamauga.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE GREAT ORATOR OF THE GILDED AGE HOUSE
In late 1863, at the personal request of Abraham Lincoln, Garfield resigned his military commission to take a seat in the United States House of Representatives. Lincoln explained that while he had plenty of capable generals in the field, he was desperately short of eloquent, courageous champions who could defend his war policies and emancipation on the floor of Congress. For the next seventeen years, James A. Garfield served as the intellectual leader of the House of Representatives, rising to become Minority Leader.

Garfield was the finest parliamentary debater of his generation. While other politicians relied on florid theatrical bombast or bitter personal invective, Garfield's speeches were encyclopedic, logical, and morally compelling, marshaling economic data, historical precedent, and classical philosophy with effortless grace. He was an unyielding champion of sound money, hard currency, and Black civil rights, fiercely condemning white violence in the South. When Roscoe Conkling's Stalwart faction attempted to turn the Republican Party into a patronage cartel, Garfield remained a principled independent, navigating the treacherous waters between Stalwarts and reformers. By 1880, the Ohio state legislature had elected Garfield to the United States Senate. He looked forward to a long, dignified career as an elder statesman in the Senate chamber. But destiny had other plans.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE DEADLOCK AT THE EXPOSITION BUILDING
In June 1880, fifteen thousand spectators crammed into the cavernous Interstate Exposition Building in Chicago for the Republican National Convention. The convention was deadlocked in a titanic, venomous factional war. Senator Roscoe Conkling arrived at the head of three hundred and six unyielding Stalwart delegates dedicated to nominating former President Ulysses S. Grant for an unprecedented third term. Opposing Grant was Senator James G. Blaine of Maine, the charismatic 'Plumed Knight' of the Half-Breed faction. James A. Garfield attended the convention as the delegation chairman from Ohio, tasked with placing his fellow Ohioan, Treasury Secretary John Sherman, into nomination.

Conkling opened the proceedings with an electrifying, swaggering oration for Grant, reciting from memory: 'And when asked what state he hails from, our sole reply shall be, he hails from Appomattox, and its famous apple tree!' When Garfield rose to nominate Sherman, he gave a speech of astonishing eloquence that completely captivated the hostile hall. Urging calm and unity, Garfield opened with magnificent poetry: 'I have seen the sea lashed into fury and tossed into spray, and its grandeur moves the soul of the dullest man; but I remember that it is not the billows, but the calm level of the sea from which all heights and depths are measured.' As Garfield spoke, delegates began murmuring to one another that the man on the platform, not the candidate he was nominating, should be the next President of the United States.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE THIRTY-SIXTH BALLOT: THE RELUCTANT NOMINEE
When voting began, the convention entered a historic stalemate. Ballot after ballot, Conkling's 306 Stalwarts voted like an iron wall for Grant, while Blaine and Sherman held the rest. Ten ballots passed, then twenty, then thirty. On the thirty-fourth ballot, the Wisconsin delegation suddenly cast sixteen votes for James A. Garfield. Garfield rose instantly to his feet, pale and visibly distressed, shouting to the convention chairman: 'Mr. President! I rise to a point of order! No man has a right, without the consent of the person voted for, to announce that person's name, and being here as the representative of another, I do not consent!' Chairman George Frisbie Hoar interrupted him sharply from the podium: 'The gentleman from Ohio is not stating a point of order! He will resume his seat!'

The dam had broken. On the thirty-fifth ballot, Blaine and Sherman delegates threw their strength behind Garfield. On the thirty-sixth ballot, a tidal wave swept the hall: Garfield received 399 votes, shattering the deadlock and securing the nomination. Stunned and trembling, Garfield sat in his chair with his head in his hands, muttering to friends: 'This is terrible. I never sought this.' To appease the furious Conkling and his 306 Grant delegates, the convention nominated Conkling's henchman, Chester A. Arthur, for vice president. In November 1880, after a masterful 'Front Porch Campaign' from his farm in Mentor, Ohio, James A. Garfield defeated Union General Winfield Scott Hancock by just 1,898 popular votes, becoming the twentieth President of the United States. He was fifty years old, at the absolute summit of his powers. But waiting in the shadows was a delusional, deranged lawyer clutching a British bulldog revolver.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
James A. Garfield's rise from wilderness poverty and canal boats to the presidency was the quintessential embodiment of the American dream. He brought a brilliant intellect, battlefield courage, and moral vision to the Executive Mansion. Next week, we examine the heartbreaking climax of Garfield's life: the morning at the Baltimore and Potomac train station, the madman Charles Guiteau, Alexander Graham Bell's metal detector, and the agonizing 79-day struggle that broke the nation's heart. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
